title: The Debye-Hückel Theory
lead: Activity coefficients of ions can be estimated instead of measured. Debye and Hückel pictured each ion surrounded by a cloud of opposite charge whose size depends on every ion in the solution, which also explains why charged colloidal particles stay dispersed.
notes: The book prints no credits for this page; Figure 25.6.1 is by Roland1952 (CC BY-SA 3.0), Figure 25.6.2 by Petergans (public domain) and Figure 25.6.3 by Larryisgood (CC BY-SA 3.0).
exercise_notes: The book sets no exercise here; both exercises are new and AI-written, with AI solutions, and their answers were checked by computation.

exercises.source_id: If there are other ions present the ionic strength involves
exercises.prompt: A solution is 0.010 mol/kg in CaCl2 and 0.020 mol/kg in NaCl. Find (a) its ionic strength and (b) the size $1/κ$ of the ionic atmosphere, using the book's $κ = 3.29\sqrt{I}$ nm−1 for water at 25 °C.

parts.hint: List every ion with its molality: Cl⁻ comes from both salts.

answer.solution:
(a) The ions are Ca2+ at 0.010 mol/kg, Na+ at 0.020 mol/kg and Cl− at 0.020 + 0.020 = 0.040 mol/kg. Then $I = \tfrac{1}{2}\left[(0.010)(2)^2 + (0.020)(1)^2 + (0.040)(1)^2\right] = \tfrac{1}{2}(0.10) = 0.050$ mol/kg.

(b) $κ = 3.29\sqrt{0.050} = 0.736$ nm−1, so $1/κ = 1.36$ nm. The calcium ions, a third of the ions in number, supply 40% of the ionic strength because their charge enters squared.

exercises.source_id: Unfortunately this theory only works at very low concentrations
exercises.prompt: Estimate the mean ionic activity coefficient of 0.0010 mol/kg ZnSO4 in water at 25 °C from the limiting law, $\log_{10}γ_\pm = -A|z_+z_-|\sqrt{I}$ with $A = 0.51$.

answer.hint: Work out the ionic strength first: both ions carry a charge of magnitude 2.
answer.solution: $I = \tfrac{1}{2}\left[(0.0010)(2)^2 + (0.0010)(2)^2\right] = 0.0040$ mol/kg, four times the molality. With $|z_+z_-| = 4$, $\log_{10}γ_\pm = -(0.51)(4)\sqrt{0.0040} = -0.129$, so $γ_\pm = 0.74$. A 1:1 salt at the same molality would have $γ_\pm = 0.96$: the doubled charges matter far more than the concentration here.

footnotes.html: The Debye length is $1/κ$, the size of the cloud, and $κ$ is its inverse. Below, where the book says the Debye length and $\ln γ_\pm$ are proportional, $\ln γ_\pm$ is proportional to $κ$, the inverse of the Debye length.
The unit printed as mol<sup>−1</sup>/2dm<sup>3/2</sup> is mol<sup>−1/2</sup> dm<sup>3/2</sup>, so that $A\sqrt{I}$ and $Ba_0\sqrt{I}$ are pure numbers with $I$ in mol/dm<sup>3</sup>.

Equation 25.6.1, with its denominator $1 + Ba_0\sqrt{I}$, is the extended Debye–Hückel equation of Section 25.7. The limiting law is its form at very low ionic strength, $\log_{10}γ_\pm = -A|z_+z_-|\sqrt{I}$. For the mean activity coefficient of a salt the charge factor is $|z_+z_-|$; $z_j^2$ belongs to the activity coefficient of a single ion $j$.
The logarithm of the mean activity coefficient, $\log γ_\pm$, is proportional to $\sqrt{I}$; $γ_\pm$ itself is not.
The horizontal axis is the square root of the ionic strength, $\sqrt{I}$, though the image labels it ionic strength. Only against $\sqrt{I}$ is the limiting law a straight line of slope −0.51.
The image shows no plot of potential against distance. It draws a gold nanoparticle with a layer of cations bound to its surface and a looser cloud of cations and anions around it.
